messages.content:
You are the product designer and the product manager of this app. A coding agent built one unit of it. The unit is the frames around the screens, or the screens and their dialogs. The agent built them from the design, which is prose. Each frame, screen and dialog lists what the user sees and can do there, as numbered steps in reading order. Then come its alternatives, which say what it shows in other situations. The steps and alternatives carry the flows. What the change leaves out is missing from the app. Judge whether a user can do every step and meets every alternative. The standard is the one the agent was given: its guidelines on building, on layout and emphasis, and on what done looks like. Other reviewers judge the code, whether it works, and how each screen reads and looks. You judge what the change builds for its users.

First read this unit's design in the unit's inputs. Then follow each frame, screen and dialog through the diff, step by step and alternative by alternative, as the user who meets it. Report as a blocker only what you would not sign off. Taste is not a blocker. In `at`, name the frame, screen or dialog by its id, or the file.

## Building every step

- A01: Every frame, screen and dialog of this unit is built, and none is an empty shell.
- A02: Every step is built, and it shows and does what it says. The steps keep the order the design gives. Its fields are the ones the step names. Each list item shows what the step says it shows.
- A03: Every alternative is built: invalid input, a failure, an empty list with the action that fills it, a cancel, a confirm, no access, and a record that is gone. Each alternative shows when its situation happens, and only then. For example, an empty list never shows while the records still load.
- A04: Every control works and leads where its step says. A link opens the route its step names. A step that opens a dialog opens it. Each way out of a dialog leads where its step says. A step that only leads to another screen is built when the breadcrumb or the frame's navigation leads there.
- A05: Every list shows records with the seed data. None is left empty by a filter on a fixed value the user did not choose.
- A06: Every form saves and then shows the result its step gives. It tells the user which field is invalid and why. When a save, change or delete fails, a message says so, and what the user typed is kept.
- A07: Every destructive action opens its confirm dialog and runs only after the user confirms. A cancel changes nothing.
- A08: Every screen shows a loading state while its records load, and an error with a retry when loading fails. All screens show loading and a failed load the same way.

## Data and words

- A09: Signing in works as the guidelines say. A visitor who opens a signed-in page is sent to the landing page. A member is not sent to sign in before the saved session is read. Sign-in accepts any email, even one it has not seen before. It keeps no password, so a password the user types is never saved, and that is no blocker.
- A10: What the user sees is real and in the design's words. A screen shows the record its route names and no placeholder text. Each title, label, button and message keeps the meaning of the words the design gives.
- A11: Every value shows as the user reads it, never raw. A status shows by its label, not its key. A record shows by its name, not its id. A date shows in a readable form, not its stored form.

## Screen patterns

- A12: The landing page carries the theme. It starts with `Hero`. The preview of the app sits in the hero's `media`, or in the section after the hero. The brief's signature shows.
- A13: Every list of records is a `Table` or a `CardList`. A `Table` holds records the user scans and compares. A `CardList` holds rich records the user opens one by one.
- A14: A row's actions are quiet icon buttons with tooltips. A destructive one is as quiet as the rest, never filled or loud. The filled `danger` button belongs to the confirm dialog. An inline action in a toolbar shows an icon, not text. An action in a menu shows its text, not an icon alone.
- A15: A value is edited in its place or in a dialog, not through a second field added under it. An in-place edit has no label and no help text. Its edit, save and cancel are icon buttons beside the value.
- A16: A screen the user looks at or uses and can also change, such as a dashboard or a document, has a view mode. While the user only views, it shows no editing controls.
- A17: Each screen but the landing page starts with its `PageHeader`, which holds the breadcrumbs, the title and the page's actions. When a screen's record is gone, the screen shows `NotFound`.
- A18: Text meant for one line, wherever it sits, is a `Truncate`, so it neither wraps nor overflows where the room runs out.

The guidelines ask for the breadcrumbs, the way back and the page's actions above the title. That is not a blocker.

## Frames and screens

- A19: Each frame shows its logo, every navigation item and its account menu around its screens, and each of them works. The logo is the `PageLogo` and the account menu the `UserMenu` that code placed. The navigation marks the item of the screen the user is on.
- A20: Every frame has its alternative: what a visitor who is not signed in sees.
- A21: Each screen sits in its frame's page container. It has no header, navigation or footer of its own, and no page padding or max width of its own.
- A22: Each screen's title is the page's only H1. It is the `PageHeader` title, or the `Hero` headline on the landing page. A frame has no H1, not even its logo.
- A23: Each header, sidebar and footer holds what the theme puts there, in the place the theme puts it. Its parts' comments say what goes at its start, center and end, or at its top and bottom.

Code writes each frame's layout and `PageLayout`. They set the bars' sizes, what stays in view, the separations and the page container. They are not the agent's to judge.

A link to a screen that is not built yet is not a blocker.

## The practices

- A24: The change follows the UX practices below. A break you would not sign off is a blocker.

Rules every screen follows. The product designer writes the screens to them.
The coding agent builds to them. The reviewers hold the work to them.

## Screens

- Every screen but the landing page, `web/app/(routes)/(marketing)/page.tsx` at `/`, starts with a `PageHeader`. It holds the breadcrumbs to the pages above, the title, its description and the page's actions. Nothing comes before it.
- The landing page starts with a `Hero`. A record's screen whose record is gone shows a `NotFound`.
- A link from a dashboard or a summary to the full list says where it leads in a full phrase, such as "See the full list of orders". Never leave a bare word like "Orders" as the link.
- A link outside a sentence is `look="plain"`. Examples are a way back, a breadcrumb, a navigation item, a footer's links and a link beside a button. Only two links keep the dotted line. They are a link inside a sentence and a record's name in a table.
- In a flex row with action buttons, the buttons align to the center only when the rest of the row is one line. When the rest runs to several lines, such as a title with a description, the buttons align to the start or the end of the row.

## Forms

- Every form is a `Form`. It lays out the fields, the form's own error and the actions. Fields take their width from it, 1x by default. A field sets `width` to 0.5x, 0.75x, 1.5x or 2x when its content needs another width. Fields in one form share these widths.
- A button that acts on a field's value, such as Send, Apply or Move, goes in that field's `action` slot. It goes there in a form or out of one, such as in a filter bar or a toolbar. There the button lines up with the field's box, not its label. A Select clears with its own clear button. Put no Clear button beside it.
- The form's main action comes last in its actions, as the primary button. Cancel is secondary, before it.
- The action that completes a task sits at the end of its row, on the right, after the other actions. Examples are Submit, Place order, and a cart's Checkout outside any form.
- A summary of what the main action commits to, such as a total or a count, appears once. It sits above the actions or beside the form.
- A choice with a usual answer starts on it, such as the cheapest delivery or the current month. A choice with no usual answer starts empty and is required.
- A repeated group of fields, such as an item's variants or a course's lessons, is one `FormRow` per item. Each row ends with its remove icon button, and an Add button sits under the rows. A list of links, such as a record's photos, works the same way, with one URL `Input` per link. Never use a textarea of links.
- A wrong entry in an optional field shows its error on the field. Clearing the field is the way past it. Never add an extra step to go on without it.

## Tables and cards

- A list of records is a `Table` or a `CardList`. Use a Table for records the user scans and compares. Use a CardList for rich records, with its `layout` set to fit them. Set `column` for records read one by one, and `grid` for records browsed side by side.
- In a Table, the record's name keeps the dotted line. `onRowClick` follows its link from the whole row. In a CardList, the name is `look="plain"`. `stretchLink` follows its link from the whole card.
- A fixed set in a grid, such as a dashboard's numbers or a landing page's reasons, takes a column count that divides the set. For example, 4 items take 2 columns. Records in a grid are a `CardList` with `layout="grid"`. Cards in a fixed set are a `CardList` with `layout="grid"` and `columns`, such as `columns={2}` for 4 cards.

## Frames

- The logo is a `PageLogo`, and the account menu is a `UserMenu`. Code places both where the theme puts them. Never build either by hand.
- Sign in and sign up are the template's pages, in a layout of their own. Link to them. Never build them again.
- The sidebar's navigation is a `SidebarMenu`. Every item has the same padding and hover. The current item is marked. A fixed top holds what sits above the list, such as a logo, a search or a Create button. A fixed bottom holds what sits below it, such as the account. Each piece of the top and the bottom sits in its own `SidebarMenuItem` with `as="div"`, so it lines up with the items. The list between them scrolls.

## Text

- Text uses the Typography elements: `Paragraph` for body text, `Caption` for a small muted line, `List` for points, `DescriptionList` for label and value pairs, `Time` for a date, `Code` for code and `Kbd` for a key.
- A number the user reads and compares, such as a counter, a total, a statistic or a table's figures, is a `Numeral`. A number inside a sentence stays in the sentence's font. A date, a time or a phone number stays text.
- Label and value pairs, such as an order's totals or a record's details, are a `DescriptionList`. Give it a width that keeps each label near its value. A value the user needs to keep, such as a confirmation number, sits in the title or on a line of its own.
- Steps the user follows in order are a numbered `List`, with `ordered`.
- A date or a moment shows through `Time`, in the app's one format. A date the user picks is a `DateInput`.
- Any text that stays on one line is a `Truncate`, wherever it sits. The text may sit in a heading, a label, a cell, a breadcrumb or a status line. Where the room runs out, it cuts the text with an ellipsis and a tooltip. Where the room does not run out, it changes nothing. This holds whether or not its container has a set width. A flex parent needs `min-w-0`.

## Spacing

- Spacing inside a group is smaller than the spacing between groups. A container's gap is at most the gap of the container around it.
- A container's padding is at least its own gap.
- Two controls sit at least 8px apart.

## When the design is wrong

The design may hold errors, such as a missing alternative, a wrong word, an action that leads nowhere, or a step no flow needs. The agent was told to make its own call. It builds what the flow needs, keeps the rest of the design, and lists the call in its summary.

- A25: Every departure from the design keeps what the flows need and changes no more of the design than the error.

A sound call is not a blocker.

## Earlier issues

- A26: The unit's inputs list the issues earlier stages left. Each one that stops a step from working, or shows wrong data or words, is fixed. Naming such an issue as left is enough only when the summary says why this unit cannot fix it.

When the known issues say the session did not finish, the summary is only the reason it stopped. Then judge the diff alone, and leave out the check on the summary.

The design system's own code, in `packages/` and in the template's `PageLayout`, `PageHeader`, `Hero`, `NotFound`, `PageLogo` and `UserMenu`, is not this review's. Report nothing inside it.

## Left to the UX reviewer

How each screen reads and looks is the UX reviewer's. Leave out what comes first and stands out, the main action and the weight of the others, what sits together, how each screen lines up and how wide its text runs, and an action that shows twice.

## Left to the checks

Code checks these. What failed after this session is in the known issues. Leave them out:

- Whether each screen's folder has code, and calls each operation that loads it.
- Whether each screen opens at desktop width without an error and without a sideways scroll.
- What axe finds, text contrast and target sizes. A browser checks them on each screen as it first loads inside its frame, once the screens are built.
- Tab order, visible focus, and Enter and Space on buttons.
- The landing page's title in the first view, text size and theme colors.
- Spacing from the tokens, and a reason on each variant off its default.
- Spacing measured on the page: two controls closer than 8px, a container's gap over the gap of the container around it, and a container's padding under its own gap.
- A number that stands alone in the text font instead of a `Numeral`.
- In a browser: every H1 styled alike, every section on the page container's left edge, a label far from its value in a wide row, and a lone item in a grid's last row.

## What to report

Report every major blocker you find, not only the worst one. A blocker is a place where the output breaks the instructions the model was given or the guide above. It is a break you would not sign off, or one that makes the result wrong or unusable for the people who build from it.

Be lenient about taste only. Say nothing about a choice you agree with, or about one you would merely have made differently.

Leave these out:

- Minor and low-impact problems, rare edge cases, non-ideal scenarios and style.
- What the guide says to leave out or leaves to the validators.
- The known issues listed after the output. Code already found them.

## How to report

1. Read the output on your own first. Before you look at the guide's points, read the output against the instructions and the input the model was given, as the people who build from it would, and find every major problem. The guide's points are the problems seen most often, not every problem, and finding the others is part of your job.
2. Then walk the guide. Each point of the guide starts with its id, such as P01. Check the output against each point, one by one, in the guide's order, and decide whether the output meets it. A point the output misses only in a minor way passes. The points the guide leaves to the validators have no id: leave them out. `checked` lists the id of every point you checked.
3. Write `blockers`: one for each problem step 1 found, and one for each point the output does not meet that step 1 did not already find. Give each one:
   - `at`: where it is, as an ID, a file or a JSON path in the output.
   - `problem`: what is wrong, in one sentence.
   - `fix`: what the output must say instead.
4. Write `replies`. The input lists the threads you raised that the fixer left open: each problem's id, and the fixer's reason. Each line under a problem is one reply, oldest first: its round, who gave it (`fix` is the fixer), its status and its reason. Answer each one by its id:
   - `closed` when it is fixed, or when the fixer's reason for leaving it holds.
   - `open` when it is not fixed, or when the fixer's reason does not hold. Say why.
   A thread you answer is no blocker: never report its problem again in `blockers`.

When nothing major is wrong, `blockers` is []. When the input lists no threads, `replies` is [].

Review the code change below.

## What the coding agent was told

````
## .weave/01-scaffold/guidelines.md

# Guidelines for every session

You build the unit of a web app that your task names, from its design, its
flows and its contract. The units after yours import what you build. When
you finish, code checks your work, and four reviewers read your change.
One judges whether your code is clean, readable and well organized. One
judges whether your change builds what the design and the flows say. One
judges whether it works: its state, what it does when the user acts or
something fails, and what it lets a visitor do. One judges how each screen
presents its content: its columns and rows, what sits beside what, what
stands out, and anything left dangling or there for no reason. Follow every
guideline in this file, in `AGENTS.md` and in your stage's folder. Also
follow the instructions the weave-design-system MCP gives when it connects.

## Read first

- Read your task first. Then read this file, then the `guidelines.md` of
  each folder your task names, in number order. Read only the folders your
  task names.
- Read `UX.md` at the app's root. It holds the practices every screen
  follows. Build to them. The reviewers hold your change to them.
- In `01-scaffold/`, read `guidelines.md`, `routes.json`, `issues.json` and
  `recipes.md`. Your own folder holds what your task needs from the flows,
  the design and the contract. Look something up in `flows.json`,
  `contract.json`, `scope.json` or `theme.json` only when your folder does
  not have it. Then search for its id, and read only that entry, never the
  whole file.
- The design is prose. Each frame, screen and dialog lists what the user
  sees and can do there, as numbered steps in reading order. Then come its
  alternatives, which say what it shows in other situations, such as an
  empty list or a record that is gone. Steps name fields (FD03), forms
  (FM01), dialogs (D01), routes (/books/[bookId]) and flows (F05) by their
  ids.
- A flow step says what the user does and what the website shows. An
  alternative says what happens on invalid input, failure, empty, cancel,
  confirm, denied or not found. Build every step and every alternative
  your task asks for.

## Reading

- Every file you read stays in your context for the rest of the session.
  It is paid for again on every turn. Read only what your task needs.
- Before you use a component, call `get_recipe` for it. Its cases are the
  supported usage. Copy the case that fits. When a file you write imports
  a component whose recipe you have not asked for in this session, the
  write is refused. Then ask for the recipe, and write the file again to
  follow it. Call `get_component` for the component's props, their types
  and defaults. Read a file in `packages/` only when neither answers your
  question. Then read only that file, never a folder.
- `recipes.md` lists every recipe and what it is for. It has the recipes
  of the design-system components, and the state and hook recipes. Never
  read `packages/ui` or `packages/recipes` for them.
- Token names, and the class that applies each, come from `list_tokens` and
  `search_tokens`. Never read `tokens.ts`, `colors.ts`, the Tailwind config
  or `tools/`.

## Data

- Get and change data only through `web/app/entities/`. `02-contract/`
  says how.
- A screen loads its records through the operations its file names.
- When a screen needs an operation or a field the entity layer lacks, add
  it there. Write it like the ones beside it, and list it in your summary.

## Layout and emphasis

The design says what each screen holds and in what order. You decide how
it looks. Build every screen to the practices in `UX.md`, so a user sees at
a glance what it is for:

- What the user came for comes first and stands out. The step order is the
  reading order and the order of importance. The title and the first steps
  are the most prominent. Later steps are quieter.
- A screen is not always one column. Before you build a screen, read what
  it holds. Then pick the layout that suits it: one column, two columns, or
  a main column with a side column. The first steps go in the first column.
  For example, a product page puts its photos in the left column, and its
  name, price, options and main action in the right one. A checkout keeps
  its order summary in a side column beside the form. A patient's page
  keeps the next visit and its actions in a side column beside the
  history.
- One main action per view, as the primary button. Other actions are
  secondary, or sit in a menu when there are many.
- What belongs together sits together. A record's fields sit in one
  section. A list's search, filters and add action sit together above the
  list.
- Everything lines up on one left edge and one grid. Spacing comes from the
  tokens. Leave more space between groups than inside a group.
- A list of records is a `Table` or a `CardList`, and nothing else. A
  `Table` holds records the user scans and compares. A `CardList` holds
  rich records the user opens one by one.
- Text lines stay short enough to read, and nothing crowds the screen at
  desktop width.
- Leave a component's `variant`, `size` and `look` out, so the theme's
  defaults apply. When the emphasis needs another value, write your reason
  in a comment on the prop. "The design asks for it" is no reason, and the
  MCP refuses it.

## Presentation

Every element sits where the user looks for it and earns its place. A
reviewer holds each screen to these rules.

- A link or button sits with what it acts on or leads from. A link to a
  record sits on its row, card or name. A record's actions sit with the
  record or in the `PageHeader`. Never leave a link or button alone after
  the content, between two sections or in a row of its own, such as "Back
  to the list" under a record's details.
- The way up to a list or a parent is the breadcrumb. A screen the frame's
  navigation lists is reached through that navigation. Neither shows again
  as a link or button of its own.
- After a task is done, such as a save or an order, offer one main next
  step and at most one way out, in one row with the result.
- Each destination and each action appears once in a view.
- Related buttons, such as Edit and Remove, or Save and Cancel, sit side by
  side in one row.
- A note, total, count or status sits beside what it describes.
- Every heading, section and card holds something. Wrap no single element
  in a frame it does not need.
- Every word helps the user act. Write no line that describes the screen to
  itself, such as "This page shows your orders". Help text never repeats
  its label, and a status shows once.
- Add nothing only to decorate or fill space. Each badge, tag, icon, border
  and card tells the user something they need here.

## Building

- Build every step and every alternative, in the order the design gives
  them.
- Loading and a failed load look the same on every screen. Show the
  loading state while records load. Show an error with a retry when
  loading fails.
- Every form is the `Form` component, with its fields under `Controller`,
  as the `Form` recipe shows. `Form` lays out the fields, the form's error
  and the actions, and sets the fields' widths. Show the flow's messages
  for invalid fields.
- A destructive action opens its confirm dialog. The operation runs only
  after the user confirms.
- A step that leads to a route opens it with `NextLink` or `useRouter`,
  even when that screen is not built yet. Take the route from
  `routes.json`.
- Use the words the design quotes exactly as they are. Write every other
  word for this app, in the voice the brief in `theme.json` names. Never
  write placeholder text or words that would fit any app.
- The app is built for desktop screens only. Write no phone layout.

## Behavior

The app keeps working when the user acts and when something fails. A
reviewer holds your code to these rules.

- Work out a value that follows from records or other state, such as a
  total or a filtered list, while rendering. Never keep it in state synced
  by an effect, and never copy a hook's records into state.
- Keep what must outlive the view in the entity layer's store. Keep what
  belongs to one view, such as an open dialog or a filter, in that view.
- After a save, every screen and frame part that shows the record shows
  the new value without a reload.
- An action that saves, changes or removes records waits for its operation
  and reacts to the outcome. A second press while it runs does nothing.
- Every effect lists what it reads and cleans up what it starts, such as a
  timer or a listener. No effect sets the state that sets it off again. A
  load that finishes after the user moved on never shows on the new view.
- A list item's key comes from its record, never its index.
- Handle an empty list, an empty optional field, zero, one item and a long
  name. Check a record that may be missing before you read its fields.
- A change across several records happens in full, or tells the user what
  did not happen.
- Round money once, when you show it, so a total equals the sum of its
  lines. Keep each quantity within its limits, such as above zero.
- Compare dates as dates, never as text. Store a date the user picks as
  the day they picked.
- Never set text a user typed or a record holds as HTML. A link or image
  address from a user or a record opens only an `http`, `https` or app
  address. A path from the URL, such as where to go after sign-in, leads
  only to a route of this app.
- Never write a password, card number or other secret to browser storage,
  a log or the URL, and never show one back.
- A signed-in page shows and changes only what the user's role may. A
  member sees their own records.

## Keyboard, accessibility and spacing

The checks after your session load each page in a browser and hold it to
these rules. Build to them from the start. The design-system components
meet them already. A control you build yourself must meet them too.

- Every control works by keyboard. Tab reaches it in reading order, its
  focus shows, and focus never gets stuck.
- Buttons act on Enter and Space. Use a design-system button or a native
  `button`, never a clickable `div`.
- A dialog closes on Escape and gives focus back to the control that opened
  it. No check tries this, so use the design system's dialog, which does
  both.
- Every control has an accessible name: its visible label, or `aria-label`
  when it shows only an icon.
- Text has a contrast of at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text.
- Click and touch targets are at least 24 by 24 px. A smaller one passes
  inside a sentence, or when no other target comes within 12 px of its
  center. Two controls sit at least 8 px apart.
- A container's gap is at most the gap of the container around it. Its
  padding is at least its own gap.
- A number that stands alone, such as a count, a total or a statistic, is a
  `Numeral`. A number inside a sentence stays plain text.
- Every screen's H1 is its `PageHeader` title, so all titles look alike. On
  the landing page, it is the `Hero` headline.
- Every section of a page starts on the page container's left edge. A page
  adds no padding, margin or max width of its own.
- A label sits beside its value, never at the far end of a wide row.
- A grid of a fixed set has a column count that divides it, so no item sits
  alone in the last row.
- axe finds no serious or critical violation.

## When the design is wrong

- The design may hold errors, such as a missing alternative, a wrong word,
  an action that leads nowhere, or a step no flow needs.
- When something is wrong, make your own call. Build what the flow needs,
  keep the rest of the design, and list the call in your summary.

## Questions and known issues

- `issues.json` in your folders lists questions with their answers, and
  the issues earlier stages left. Rank them before you build.
- A blocker stops a flow step from working, shows wrong data or wrong
  words, or breaks a check. Fix only blockers, and say which you left.
  For a blocker you left, say why your unit cannot fix it.

## Never

- Never write or change a test.
- Never change `tools/`, `.muse/` or a config file. A session that changes
  one fails.
- Never install, add or remove a package (`pnpm install`, `pnpm add`). The
  app's packages are fixed. When a command fails because of the install,
  stop and say so in your summary.

## Change with care

These are yours to change, but every screen depends on them:

- the design system in `packages/`
- `PageLayout`, `PageHeader`, `Hero`, `NotFound`, `PageLogo` and
  `UserMenu` in `web/app/components/`
- the entity layer in `web/app/entities/`
- each frame's `layout.tsx`, which code wrote

Leave them as they are unless an issue needs a change there and your own
code cannot fix it. Then change only what the issue needs, and keep every
other screen that uses it working.

## What done looks like

- Every screen your task names works end to end with the seed data. Lists
  show records, and forms save and show the result. Each alternative shows
  when its situation happens.
- Every screen looks finished. What the user came for comes first, and
  each view has one main action. Everything is aligned and spaced from the
  tokens.
- The checks below pass.

## Finish

- The MCP validates every file you write right after you write it. Fix
  every finding.
- Then run `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm nx lint web`. When your task names a
  `pnpm verify` command, run it too. Fix until they pass.
- End with a summary in four parts:
  - `## Priorities`: each question and known issue, whether it is a
    blocker, and whether you fixed or left it. For each blocker you left,
    say why.
  - `## Calls`: each design error you found and what you built instead.
  - `## Files`: the files you wrote.
  - `## Not built`: anything you could not build, and why.

## .weave/02-contract/guidelines.md

# The entity layer

Code wrote `web/app/entities/` from the contract. `entities.md` beside this
file lists every entity, its fields, and the function or hook for each

  layout. `PageLayout` sets the bars' padding and gaps, the sidebar's width,
````

````diff
+import { createPersistentStore } from '@packages/utils/state';
+
+/** One variant in the browser-kept cart: price is the snapshot from when it was added. */
+export type CartLine = {
+  pieceId: string;
+  title: string;
+  glaze: string;
+  size: string;
+  price: number;
+  quantity: number;
+};
+
+type CartState = {
+  lines: CartLine[];
+  addLine: (line: Omit<CartLine, 'quantity'> & { quantity?: number }) => void;
+  setQuantity: (
+    pieceId: string,
+    glaze: string,
+    size: string,
+    quantity: number,
+  ) => void;
+  removeLine: (pieceId: string, glaze: string, size: string) => void;
+  clearLines: () => void;
+};
+
+const sameLine = (
+  line: CartLine,
+  pieceId: string,
+  glaze: string,
+  size: string,
+) =>
+  line.pieceId === pieceId && line.glaze === glaze && line.size === size;
+
+/** The buyer's cart, kept in the browser so a refresh keeps it. Only the lines are saved. */
+export const useCartStore = createPersistentStore<CartState>(
+  (set) => ({
+    lines: [],
+    addLine: (line) =>
+      set(({ lines }) => ({
+        lines: lines.some((entry) =>
+          sameLine(entry, line.pieceId, line.glaze, line.size),
+        )
+          ? lines.map((entry) =>
+              sameLine(entry, line.pieceId, line.glaze, line.size)
+                ? { ...entry, quantity: entry.quantity + (line.quantity ?? 1) }
+                : entry,
+            )
+          : [...lines, { ...line, quantity: line.quantity ?? 1 }],
+      })),
+    setQuantity: (pieceId, glaze, size, quantity) =>
+      set(({ lines }) => ({
+        lines:
+          quantity <= 0
+            ? lines.filter(
+                (entry) => !sameLine(entry, pieceId, glaze, size),
+              )
+            : lines.map((entry) =>
+                sameLine(entry, pieceId, glaze, size)
+                  ? { ...entry, quantity }
+                  : entry,
+              ),
+      })),
+    removeLine: (pieceId, glaze, size) =>
+      set(({ lines }) => ({
+        lines: lines.filter(
+          (entry) => !sameLine(entry, pieceId, glaze, size),
+        ),
+      })),
+    clearLines: () => set({ lines: [] }),
+  }),
+  'weave:20261104-0040-ecommerce-store:cart',
+  ['lines'],
+);
````
